sources.news_title: US Central Command says it disabled cargo ship in Gulf of Oman
sources.text:
US Central Command says it disabled cargo ship in Gulf of Oman
U.S. Central Command says it disabled the St. Kitts-flagged cargo vessel M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman with precision strikes after its crew repeatedly ignored warnings and attempted to breach the U.S. naval blockade of Iran. CENTCOM said the ship had called at an Iranian port and was trying to leave regional waters, and that its civilian crew was warned to evacuate the areas targeted. The command says blockade operations since July have redirected 147 compliant vessels and disabled five that refused orders, and that U.S. forces have also destroyed 10 Iranian oil tankers it links to an IRGC maritime network. Separately, Iranian state media reported explosions in several coastal locations, while the IRGC Navy claimed two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines; reports did not establish whether these events were connected to the U.S. strike.

sources.news_title: U.S. Military Disables Ship After Crew Tries to Break Iran Blockade
sources.text:
The U.S. military just delivered a hard warning to any ship that thinks America’s blockade against Iran is optional.
American forces disabled the St. Kitts-flagged cargo vessel M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after its civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and tried multiple times to violate the blockade.
Here is the operation:
CENTCOM forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Nov. 7, after the ship’s civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times. A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St.… pic.twitter.com/NS5PzRmYkS
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) November 7, 2026
According to U.S. Central Command, the Huda had visited an Iranian port and was trying to leave regional waters when the enforcement action took place. American forces first directed the crew to abandon the spaces that would be targeted.
A U.S. military aircraft then fired precision munitions at the ship’s stern, disabling the vessel. That is targeted force with a clear purpose: stop the ship, protect the civilian crew as much as possible, and enforce the blockade instead of issuing empty warnings.
CENTCOM said 147 commercial vessels have complied with American orders and been redirected since July. Five merchant ships that refused to comply have been disabled, while U.S. forces have also destroyed 10 Iranian commercial oil tankers tied to what the command described as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ multibillion-dollar shadow network.
The region’s air-power posture is visible, too. CENTCOM showed an Air Force crew chief preparing an A-10C Thunderbolt II for takeoff from a Middle East base on Friday; the command did not identify that aircraft as the one used against the Huda.
A U.S. Air Force crew chief directs a U.S. Air Force A-10C Thunderbolt II in preparation for take-off from a base in the Middle East. pic.twitter.com/F0SyAHWM96
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) November 6, 2026
The Associated Press reported that the blockade has been enforced for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway that carries a major share of global oil traffic. The report also noted that the last publicly confirmed American strike on a cargo vessel came nearly a month earlier.
This is broader than one ship. Washington is squeezing Tehran by sea while also pursuing the people, equipment and money behind Iran’s nuclear and military networks.
That pressure campaign now includes a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, personnel and related movements.
Rewards for Justice is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above.… pic.twitter.com/ruTNlZxqFh
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) November 7, 2026
The choice for commercial crews is now brutally simple: follow lawful U.S. military directions and sail away, or test a blockade that American forces have repeatedly shown they are prepared to enforce.

sources.text:
An American military aircraft fired on and disabled a commercial vessel that tried to break the U.S. blockade of Iran on Saturday (November 7, 2026), U.S. Central Command said.
The St. Kitts-flagged cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port, and a U.S. plane fired precision munitions at its stern after U.S. forces directed the crew to abandon targeted spaces, Central Command said.
Building on a months-long naval blockade on Iran, the U.S. military also said on Saturday (November 7, 2026) it is launching a task force to crack down on Tehran’s movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material over its land borders and through the Caspian Sea.
Central Command estimated that its naval blockade has prevented Iran from exporting more than $25 billion in crude oil.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been threatening to carry out a new offensive against Iran. Tehran has threatened broad retaliation against Gulf infrastructure, putting countries in the region on edge.

US military fires on commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman after it attempts to breach Iran blockade
sources.text:
US military fires on commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman after it attempts to breach Iran blockade
US forces disabled a St Kitts-flagged vessel after it ignored warnings and attempted to leave the region following a visit to an Iranian port.
U.S. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port.
U.S. forces have been enforcing a naval blockade on Iran for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial strategic waterway for shipping, including of oil. The last confirmed U.S. strike on a cargo vessel was nearly a month ago in the Gulf of Oman.
Saturday’s disclosure comes in the wake of at least two instances in which U.S. Central Command did not announce military strikes it has taken in the region and officials at the command declined to confirm strikes when asked about local reports of explosions.
Also Read: 'Will attack without geographic limits': Iran's fresh warning to US after Trump's threats
Iran state media also reported on Saturday evening the sound of explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several explosions in the port of Jask. It wasn’t immediately clear what the cause of the explosions was and the U.S. military didn't immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. military had carried out new limited strikes against Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system. Trump described the military action to reporters as “minor.” U.S. Central Command ultimately didn’t comment on the action even after the strikes were confirmed by Trump.
For weeks now, Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections. The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.

sources.news_title: CENTCOM disables commercial cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman
sources.text:
U.S. forces fired a missile at a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman Saturday after the ship visited an Iranian port and attempted to leave, U.S. Central Command said.
CENTCOM alleged that the St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda attempted to violate the U.S. naval blockade.
Before U.S. aircraft disabled the ship, CENTCOM said they “directed crew to abandon targeted spaces.” CENTCOM forces fired at the stern of the ship.
“Enforcement actions since July have resulted in U.S. forces redirecting 147 commercial vessels that complied and disabled five merchant ships that refused to comply,” CENTCOM wrote.
Earlier on Saturday, CENTCOM announced that Adm. Brad Cooper had directed the formation of a new Tampa, Fla., based task force intended to control the flow of materials across Iran’s land borders.
Task Force Iron Gate aims to prevent “the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea,” according to CENTCOM.

sources.news_title: US military says it disables cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman attempting to violate blockade - The Tribune
sources.text:
Washington, DC [US], November 8 (ANI): United States Central Command (CENTCOM) forces have disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman using precision airstrikes after the ship's crew repeatedly ignored warnings and attempted to breach an active naval blockade against Iran, the US military confirmed in an official statement.
According to a press release issued by CENTCOM on Saturday, a US military aircraft deployed precision-guided munitions targeting the stern of the St. Kitts-flagged vessel M/V Huda to render it immobile.
The strike was carried out after CENTCOM personnel issued direct instructions to the civilian crew to evacuate the targeted sections of the ship to avert loss of life.
"U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Nov. 7, after the ship’s civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times," the military command stated.
The cargo vessel was intercepted as it attempted to transit out of regional waters after calling at an Iranian port.
CENTCOM highlighted that it is maintaining a rigorous enforcement posture regarding the maritime embargo imposed on Iran.
According to official US military data, blockade enforcement operations underway since July have resulted in US forces redirecting 147 commercial vessels that complied with interdiction protocols, while disabling five merchant vessels that refused to halt.
Furthermore, CENTCOM forces have previously destroyed 10 Iranian commercial oil tankers identified as key operational assets within the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' (IRGC) multibillion-dollar maritime shadow network.
Issuing a stern advisory following the maritime strike, the US military warned all commercial operators navigating the region: "All mariners transiting near Iranian coastal areas or surrounding waters are advised to heed blockade warnings from U.S. forces."
Meanwhile, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) has announced the establishment of a new task force to disrupt Iran's alleged use of ground transit routes for transporting advanced weapons, dual-use technologies and other sanctioned materials, as Washington seeks to tighten restrictions on Tehran's military supply networks (ANI)
(This content is sourced from a syndicated feed and is published as received. The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

JERUSALEM (AP) — U.S. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port.
U.S. forces have been enforcing a naval blockade on Iran for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial strategic waterway for global shipping, including of oil. The last confirmed U.S. strike on a cargo vessel was nearly a month ago in the Gulf of Oman.
Saturday’s disclosure comes in the wake of at least two instances in which U.S. Central Command did not announce military strikes it has taken in the region and officials at the command declined to confirm strikes when asked about local reports of explosions.
Iran state media also reported on Saturday evening the sound of explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several explosions in the port of Jask. It wasn’t immediately clear what the cause of the explosions was and the U.S. military didn’t immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
The Iranian military said late Saturday that two tankers had hit mines in the Hormuz area and caught fire. It did not identify the tankers’ flags or destinations.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. military had carried out new limited strikes against Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system. Trump described the military action to reporters as “minor.” U.S. Central Command ultimately didn’t comment on the action even after the strikes were confirmed by Trump.
For weeks now, Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, which were held on Nov. 3. The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.
The more than 8-month-old war has rattled global markets and diplomacy to end it has stalled. October saw the most attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since March, as Iran has tried to ramp up economic pressure on the U.S. to get it to lift its blockade.
___
Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin contributed from Washington.

Strait of Hormuz: US Central Command disables St Kitts-flagged ship after Iran port visit
US Central Command said it disabled a St Kitts-flagged ship late Saturday after it ignored repeated warnings and tried to leave the area following a visit to an Iranian port. The incident comes amid a months-long Iran naval blockade around the Strait of Hormuz and reports of unexplained explosions in the region.
AP US Central Command said late Saturday that US forces disabled a St Kitts-flagged ship. The command said the vessel ignored repeated warnings. It also said the ship tried to leave the area after calling at an Iranian port. The incident happened during months of US enforcement activity near the Strait of Hormuz.
The Strait of Hormuz is a key route for global shipping, including oil cargoes. US forces have enforced what AP described as a naval blockade on Iran there and nearby waters. The most recent confirmed US strike on a cargo vessel was nearly a month ago. That strike took place in the Gulf of Oman.
US Central Command strikes and Strait of Hormuz blockade
The ship disclosure came after reports that US Central Command did not publicise at least two earlier strikes. In those cases, officials at the command also declined to confirm strikes. The denials came after questions about local accounts of explosions. The pattern has raised questions about how the command reports operations.
Iran state media said on Saturday evening that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. Qeshm Island lies in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian outlets also reported several explosions at the port of Jask. The cause of the reported blasts was not immediately known based on available information.
Donald Trump comments on US Central Command action on Iran
The US military did not immediately reply to an Associated Press request for comment. The silence came as US President Donald Trump spoke about separate military action. Trump said on Friday that the US military carried out new limited strikes against Iran. Trump said the target was an Iranian air defense system.
Trump described the action to reporters as minor. However, US Central Command did not comment on the operation. The lack of comment continued even after Trump confirmed the strikes. This added to recent instances where official details were limited.
For weeks, Trump has said he was weighing a new wave of strikes on Iran. Trump linked that possibility to the period after the US midterm elections. The prospect has kept the Middle East and other regions on edge. Many have watched for signs of a return to wider operations after almost two months.
The latest ship incident and reports of blasts came amid heightened scrutiny of US actions. Central Command said the vessel was disabled after ignoring warnings and trying to depart. Iran’s media described explosions at Qeshm Island and Jask, with no clear cause given. US officials provided no immediate additional public details.
